 16350  specialty, or its equivalent. See INA sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 
 16351  214(i); 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 1184(i). The H-1B 
 16352  classification, however, is subject to annual numerical allocations, 
 16353  commonly referred to as a ``cap.'' See INA sections 214(g)(1)(A) and 
 16354  (g)(5)(C); 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A) and (g)(5)(C).\323\ For purposes of 
 16355  the H-1B numerical allocations, each fiscal year begins on October 1. 
 16356  Petitioners may not file H-1B petitions more than 6 months before the 
 16357  date of actual need for the employee.\324\ Thus, the earliest date an 
 16358  H-1B cap-subject petition may be filed for an allocation for a given 
 16359  fiscal year is April 1, 6 months prior to the start of the applicable 
 16360  fiscal year for which initial H-1B classification is sought.
 16361  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16362  
 16363      \323\ Under INA 214(g)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A), 65,000 
 16364  aliens may be issued H-1B visas or otherwise provided H-1B 
 16365  nonimmigrant status in a fiscal year. This limitation does not apply 
 16366  to aliens who have earned a master's or higher degree from a U.S. 
 16367  institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. 1001(a), 
 16368  until the number of aliens who are exempted from such numerical 
 16369  limitation during such year exceeds 20,000. INA 214(g)(5)(C), 8 
 16370  U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(C).
 16371      \324\ See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(2)(i)(I).
 16372  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16373  
 16374      Many F-1 students complete a program of study or post-completion 
 16375  OPT in mid-spring or early summer. Per existing regulations, after 
 16376  completing their program or post-completion OPT, F-1 students have 60 
 16377  days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps 
 16378  necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States. See new 
 16379  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). However, because the change to H-1B status cannot 
 16380  occur until October 1, an F-1 student whose program or post-completion 
 16381  OPT expires in mid-spring has two or more months following the 60-day 
 16382  period before the authorized period of H-1B status can commence. To 
 16383  address this situation, commonly known as the ``cap-gap,'' DHS 
 16384  established regulations that automatically extended F-1 D/S and, if 
 16385  applicable, post-completion OPT employment authorization for certain F-
 16386  1 nonimmigrants until April 1 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B 
 16387  status is being requested or until the validity start date of the 
 16388  approved petition, whichever is earlier. See redesignated 8 CFR 
 16389  214.2(f)(5)(vii). The extension of F-1 D/S and OPT employment 
 16390  authorization is commonly known as the ``cap-gap extension.'' This rule 
 16391  does not change the ``cap-gap extension'' provisions; it simply removes 
 16392  the reference to D/S and makes clear that an automatic extension will 
 16393  be granted to those with a fixed period of stay.
 16394  b. F-1 Status and Authorized Employment While EOS and/or Employment 
 16395  Authorization Applications Are Pending
 16396      DHS struck ``duration of status'' from redesignated 8 CFR 
 16397  214.2(f)(5)(vii) in the proposed rule and clarified that an alien with 
 16398  F-1 status whose admission period as indicated on his or her I-94 has 
 16399  expired, but who has timely filed an EOS application, will be 
 16400  authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the end 
 16401  date of his or her admission until USCIS adjudicates the EOS 
 16402  application. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This change allows for 
 16403  ongoing authorization to continue studies as long as the student has 
 16404  timely filed his or her EOS and will not penalize students if USCIS is 
 16405  unable to adjudicate an EOS application before a student's new term or 
 16406  course of study is underway. In such cases, students will be able to 
 16407  continue pursuing their full course of study.\325\ This change is 
 16408  retained in the final rule.
 16409  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16410  
 16411      \325\ However, if the extension of stay application is received 
 16412  during the 30-day period under new paragraph 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), 
 16413  the F-1 student is authorized to continue a full course of study but 
 16414  may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other 
 16415  employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B).
 16416  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16417  
 16418      DHS did clarify the title of new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) in the 
 16419  final rule, since the automatic extension is for the authorized period 
 16420  of stay while the EOS is adjudicated, rather than an automatic EOS. The 
 16421  title changed from ``Automatic Extension of F stay and employment 
 16422  authorization. . .'' to ``Automatic extension of the authorized period 
 16423  of stay and employment authorization. . .''
 16424      The shift to a fixed date of admission has implications for various 
 16425  types of employment authorization. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16426  final rule, DSOs could authorize certain types of employment 
 16427  authorization, including on-campus employment and CPT,\326\ and 
 16428  students generally did not need to be concerned about a specific 
 16429  expiration date for their student status, and thus their employment 
 16430  authorization, because they were admitted for D/S. This rule changes 
 16431  that framework with different implications for various types of 
 16432  employment authorization.
 16433  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16434  
 16435      \326\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16436  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16437  
 16438      For on-campus employment where no EAD is needed, DHS is allowing 
 16439  aliens in F-1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus 
 16440  employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to 
 16441  exceed a period of 240 days.\327\ See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). If 
 16442  the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-
 16443  1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to 
 16444  stop engaging in on-campus employment. DHS is allowing a 240-day 
 16445  automatic extension period in order to minimize disruptions to on-
 16446  campus employment by teaching assistants, post-graduates working on 
 16447  research projects, and other positions that are integral to an F-1 
 16448  student's educational program. Note that the 240 days start after the 
 16449  expiration of one's current stay. DHS has always encouraged and will 
 16450  continue to encourage all nonimmigrants to apply for EOS within
 16451  
 16452  [[Page 45107]]
 16453  
 16454  the six months \328\ preceding the expiration of their current 
 16455  authorized stay thereby providing an additional buffer against any 
 16456  disruption of the ability to work.
 16457  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16458  
 16459      \327\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) for a description of on-campus 
 16460  employment. For on-campus employment that is based on severe 
 16461  economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances pursuant to 
 16462  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), see later discussion for 
 16463  additional restrictions. The EOS application must be timely filed 
 16464  pursuant to the new paragraph at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). 
 16465  Moreover, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay application 
 16466  during the 30-day period provided in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)(new), he 
 16467  or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized 
 16468  employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, 
 16469  and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and 
 16470  employment authorization application, if required) before engaging 
 16471  in CPT or employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16472      \328\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16473  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16474  ahead of expiration.
 16475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16476  
 16477      Likewise, DHS is allowing an automatic extension of off-campus 
 16478  employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the 
 16479  EOS application, for F-1 students who have demonstrated severe economic 
 16480  hardship pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) and previously received 
 16481  an EAD from USCIS that expired at the program end date that is now 
 16482  being extended with the EOS application. See new 8 CFR 
 16483  214.2(f)(5)(viii). These circumstances may include loss of financial 
 16484  aid or on-campus employment without fault on the part of the student, 
 16485  substantial fluctuations in the value of currency or exchange rate, 
 16486  inordinate increases in tuition and/or living costs, unexpected changes 
 16487  in the financial condition of the student's source of support, medical 
 16488  bills, or other substantial and unexpected expenses. In such cases, DHS 
 16489  believes a 240-day automatic extension of employment authorization will 
 16490  help alleviate the severe economic hardship and avoid a disruption in 
 16491  their employment, especially given the fact that an EAD is required and 
 16492  the frequency at which these students must submit an application for 
 16493  employment authorization.\329\ Additionally, given that USCIS's average 
 16494  EAD processing time is typically 60-120 days for foreign students and 
 16495  90-120 for most others, a 240-day timeframe provides sufficient 
 16496  flexibility in case of unexpected delays.
 16497  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16498  
 16499      \329\ See 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(3). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(F)(2) 
 16500  provides that employment authorization based upon severe economic 
 16501  hardship may be granted in one-year intervals up to the expected 
 16502  date of completion of the student's current course of study.
 16503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16504  
 16505      For F-1 students granted off-campus employment authorization on the 
 16506  basis of severe economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances 
 16507  pursuant to redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), DHS proposed, and is 
 16508  retaining in the final rule, an automatic extension of such employment 
 16509  authorization with a different validity period than the general 8 CFR 
 16510  214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) severe economic hardship employment authorization 
 16511  extension described above while their EOS applications are pending. See 
 16512  new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This will codify USCIS's current policy 
 16513  which states USCIS may grant SSR employment authorization for the 
 16514  duration of the Federal Register notice validity period, but the period 
 16515  of authorization may not exceed the F-1 student's academic program end 
 16516  date.\330\
 16517  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16518  
 16519      \330\ See generally USCIS Policy Manual, Vol. 2, Part F, Chap. 
 16520  6, Employment, https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-f-chapter-6 (last visited Feb. 4, 2026).
 16521  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16522  
 16523      As first promulgated in 1998, the SSR regulations provide necessary 
 16524  flexibility to address unforeseeable emergencies by allowing DHS, by 
 16525  notice in the Federal Register, to suspend the applicability of some or 
 16526  all of the requirements for on- and off-campus employment authorization 
 16527  for specified F-1 students where an emergency situation has arisen 
 16528  calling for this action. These F-1 students must continue to attend 
 16529  classes but are allowed to take a reduced course load. By regulation, 
 16530  aliens approved for SSR to take at least 6 semester or quarter hours of 
 16531  instruction at the undergraduate level or 3 semester or quarter hours 
 16532  of instruction at the graduate level. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). 
 16533  Failure to take the required credits could be considered a failure to 
 16534  maintain F-1 status. The SSR regulations are announced by notice in the 
 16535  Federal Register, and such employment may only be undertaken during the 
 16536  validity period of the SSR notice.
 16537      Due to the shift to a fixed admission period, DHS proposed to 
 16538  provide an automatic extension of SSR-based employment so aliens' 
 16539  ability to benefit from this long-standing regulatory relief is not 
 16540  interrupted by USCIS processing times. This change is consistent with 
 16541  current USCIS policy, which allows for SSR employment authorization to 
 16542  be granted for the duration of the Federal Register notice validity 
 16543  period, so long as the period of authorization may not exceed the F-1 
 16544  student's academic program end date. It is also consistent with 
 16545  existing practice for certain nonimmigrants who require an EAD.\331\ 
 16546  This is retained in the final rule. Further, DHS has retained its 
 16547  proposal to automatically extend SSR authorization if an F-1 student 
 16548  has a timely-filed EOS pending for up to the end date stated in the 
 16549  Federal Register notice announcing the suspension of certain 
 16550  requirements, or 240 days, whichever is earlier. See new 8 CFR 
 16551  214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16552  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16553  
 16554      \331\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16555  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16556  
 16557      As evidence of these automatic extensions of employment 
 16558  authorization, DHS will allow the F-1 student's I-94 (or successor 
 16559  form) or EAD (Form I-766, or successor form), for F-1 nonimmigrants 
 16560  requiring an EAD, when combined with a notice issued by USCIS 
 16561  indicating receipt of a timely filed EOS application (such as the Form 
 16562  I-797),\332\ to be considered unexpired until USCIS issues a decision 
 16563  on the EOS application, not to exceed 240 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16564  214.2(f)(5)(viii). SSR-based employment authorization that has been 
 16565  automatically extended can be evidenced by the F-1 student's EAD and 
 16566  the receipt notice issued by USCIS (the Form I-797), not to exceed the 
 16567  lesser of 240 days or the end date stated in the Federal Register 
 16568  notice announcing the suspension of certain requirements.
 16569  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16570  
 16571      \332\ However, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay 
 16572  application during the 30-day period provided in new paragraph 8 CFR 
 16573  214.2(f)(5)(v), he or she does not receive an automatic extension of 
 16574  authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic 
 16575  hardship, and must wait for approval of the extension of stay 
 16576  application (and employment authorization application, if required) 
 16577  before engaging in CPT or employment. 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16578  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16579  
 16580  5. New Process for EOS Application
 16581      Under current regulations, F-1 students may obtain a program 
 16582  extension from a DSO as long as they are maintaining status and making 
 16583  normal progress toward the completion of their educational objectives. 
 16584  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i) and (iii). The problem with the ``normal 
 16585  progress'' standard is that it is undefined, and DHS believes that 
 16586  retaining it could lead to inconsistent adjudications. Even now, the 
 16587  lack of a standard definition for normal progress leads DSOs to 
 16588  inconsistently extend F-1 students' program end dates and thus their 
 16589  stay in the United States. Some DSOs use a strict standard, evaluating, 
 16590  for example, documentation to support a student's claim of a compelling 
 16591  medical condition or illness that serves as the basis for the student's 
 16592  request for extension of the student's current program. However, other 
 16593  DSOs claim that the student is making ``normal progress'' whenever a 
 16594  student simply needs more time to complete the program. This 
 16595  inconsistency results in some students being able to remain in F-1 
 16596  status for years simply by having the DSO update the Form I-20 without 
 16597  providing a justification as to how the student is making ``normal 
 16598  progress'' and what academic or medical circumstances necessitate the 
 16599  extension of the program.
 16600      Therefore, DHS proposed not to use a ``normal progress'' standard 
 16601  with respect to seeking a program extension, and to require, in 
 16602  addition to the requirement that the applicant obtain a Form I-20 from 
 16603  the DSO recommending extension of the program, the applicant will be 
 16604  required to file an EOS
 16605  
 16606  [[Page 45108]]
 16607  
 16608  application to request additional time to complete their current course 
 16609  of study beyond their authorized period of admission. See new 8 CFR 
 16610  214.2(f)(7)(i). This change is retained in the final rule.
 16611      Apart from pursuing a new course of study, DHS appreciates that the 
 16612  time for study can legitimately fluctuate given the changing goals and 
 16613  actions of the student. For example, a student may experience 
 16614  compelling academic or medical reasons, or circumstances beyond their 
 16615  control that cause them to need additional time in the United States 
 16616  beyond the predetermined end date of the program in which they were 
 16617  initially enrolled. DHS understands these circumstances arise and 
 16618  believes these scenarios present an appropriate situation for DHS to 
 16619  directly evaluate the nonimmigrant's eligibility for additional time in 
 16620  the United States. However, instead of effectively extending their stay 
 16621  through a DSO's program extension recommendation in SEVIS, students 
 16622  will have to obtain a Form I-20 from the DSO recommending a program 
 16623  extension and apply to USCIS for an EOS. Immigration officers thereby 
 16624  will be able to conduct appropriate background and security checks on 
 16625  the applicant at the time of the EOS application and directly review 
 16626  the proffered evidence to ensure that the alien is eligible for the 
 16627  requested EOS, including through assessing whether the alien remains 
 16628  admissible. See 8 CFR 214.1(a)(3)(i). This extra step is necessary 
 16629  because an immigration officer will be able to see a more fulsome 
 16630  picture while considering the student's particular circumstances, and 
 16631  be able to identify potential fraud and criminality, thereby ensuring 
 16632  public safety and program integrity.
 16633      In these circumstances, DHS will only extend the stay beyond the 
 16634  program end date of an otherwise eligible F-1 student requesting 
 16635  additional time to complete their program if the additional time needed 
 16636  is due to a compelling academic reason, documented medical illness or 
 16637  medical condition, or circumstance that was beyond the student's 
 16638  control. As with all nonimmigrant EOS requests, an alien seeking an EOS 
 16639  generally must have continually maintained status.\333\ If an F-1 
 16640  student dropped below a full course of study, that drop must have been 
 16641  properly authorized. F-1 students seeking extensions of stay must 
 16642  primarily be seeking to temporarily stay in the United States solely to 
 16643  pursue a full course of study, INA section 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 
 16644  1101(a)(15)(F)(i), and not for other reasons separate from, or in 
 16645  addition to, pursuing a full course of study.
 16646  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16647  
 16648      \333\ Failure to file on or before the expiration of the 
 16649  previously accorded status or failure to maintain such status may be 
 16650  excused at the discretion of USCIS if the alien demonstrates that at 
 16651  the time of filing: the delay was due to extraordinary circumstances 
 16652  beyond the control of the applicant, and USCIS finds the delay 
 16653  commensurate with the circumstances, the alien has not otherwise 
 16654  violated his or her status, and is not subject to deportation. See 8 
 16655  CFR 214.1(c)(3)(viii).
 16656  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16657  
 16658      If an F-1 student were to violate the terms of his or her F-1 
 16659  status, the F-1 student would need to apply to USCIS for reinstatement, 
 16660  consistent with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(16). If a student is reinstated and his 
 16661  or her admit until date expires within 6 months, but the student is 
 16662  unable to complete his or her program of study within that time, then 
 16663  the F-1 student also would need to apply to USCIS for an EOS. In that 
 16664  scenario, the F-1 student would need to make separate requests for 
 16665  reinstatement and for EOS by submitting a separate form for each 
 16666  request, including the required filing fee for each form, by marking 
 16667  reinstatement on one form and then EOS on the other. Both forms can 
 16668  then be submitted together at the same time to avoid unnecessary 
 16669  adjudication delays. In the event both forms are submitted together, 
 16670  and the F-1 student's application to reinstate student status is 
 16671  denied, his or her application for EOS would also be denied, with both 
 16672  filing fees being retained by USCIS and not refunded.
 16673      By way of illustration, a student with a fixed date of admission 
 16674  may request an additional 4 months to complete his or her program 
 16675  because the student was authorized to drop below a full course of study 
 16676  for one semester due to illness. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16677  final rule, the student would need to request an updated Form I-20 from 
 16678  the DSO recommending a program extension. Now, consistent with the

 16679  proposal in the NPRM, an immigration officer could review the proffered 
 16680  evidence and ensure that the claim is supported by documentation from a 
 16681  medical doctor. Conversely, a student may request an EOS for additional 
 16682  time to complete an associate program but fail to submit evidence they 
 16683  were properly authorized to drop below a full course of study. The 
 16684  immigration officer has discretion to request transcripts from the 
 16685  student. If a student's transcripts reflect that the student failed 
 16686  multiple classes one semester, an immigration officer could determine 
 16687  if the student has failed to maintain status due to a failure to carry 
 16688  a full course of study as required. In another example, a student could 
 16689  submit an EOS request to continue in the same program because he or she 
 16690  was unable to take all the required classes for his or her major due to 
 16691  over-enrollment at the school. Again, an officer could request 
 16692  additional information, if needed, to determine that the student was 
 16693  maintaining a full course of study (or, if not, was properly authorized 
 16694  to reduce his or her course load), but due to the school's high 
 16695  enrollment, the student may validly require an additional semester to 
 16696  complete the degree requirements in order to graduate.
 16697      Therefore, DHS proposed to eliminate a reference to ``normal 
 16698  progress'' with respect to seeking a program extension, and incorporate 
 16699  a new standard clarifying that acceptable reasons for requesting an 
 16700  extension of a stay for additional time to complete a program are: (1) 
 16701  compelling academic reasons; (2) a documented illness or medical 
 16702  condition; or (3) exceptional circumstances beyond the control of the 
 16703  alien. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C).\334\ These provisions are 
 16704  retained in the final rule.
 16705  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16706  
 16707      \334\ DHS did not propose to update the term ``normal progress'' 
 16708  as defined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). The provision at 8 CFR 
 16709  214.2(f)(6)(i)(E) relates to study at an approved private elementary 
 16710  or middle school or public or private academic high school. In that 
 16711  context, it is clear that ``normal progress'' is the completion of 
 16712  the academic year (for example, 6th grade).
 16713  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16714  
 16715      The first two factors are based on the current regulatory 
 16716  provisions for program extension, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii), from the 2025 
 16717  text (e.g., changes of major or research topics, and unexpected 
 16718  research problems). DHS proposed to clarify that, in addition to 
 16719  academic probation and suspension, a student's repeated inability or 
 16720  unwillingness to complete his or her course of study, as demonstrated 
 16721  by a pattern of failing classes and requesting multiple program 
 16722  extension, is not an acceptable reason to request an EOS for additional 
 16723  time to complete a program. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1). This is 
 16724  also retained in the final rule.
 16725      DHS expects bona fide students to be committed to their studies, 
 16726  attending classes as required, carrying a full course of study, and 
 16727  making reasonable efforts toward program completion. Repeatedly failing 
 16728  classes demonstrates that the student is not making reasonable efforts 
 16729  toward completing his or her program of study. Therefore, a student who 
 16730  has a pattern of failing classes that has resulted in multiple program 
 16731  extensions would not be qualified for an EOS. The prohibition against 
 16732  requesting an EOS would not include students, such as those who, 
 16733  pursuant to DHS regulations, are making normal progress toward 
 16734  completing their program of study and still may not complete the 
 16735  program within 4 years
 16736  
 16737  [[Page 45109]]
 16738  
 16739  due to the standard timeline and requirements for the program. Absent 
 16740  such factors as being placed on academic probation or suspension, or 
 16741  repeatedly failing classes, these students would be eligible for 
 16742  extension based upon compelling academic reasons. This prohibition also 
 16743  does not include cases where the DSO properly authorized the student to 
 16744  drop below a full course of study as well as cases in which the status 
 16745  has been reinstated following a loss of status. In such case, the 
 16746  student is eligible for reinstatement if the reduced course load was 
 16747  within the DSO's power to authorize. A student would be expected to 
 16748  provide evidence demonstrating the compelling academic reason in order 
 16749  for the DSO to recommend a program extension. The student may then 
 16750  apply for an EOS. While a letter from the student may be sufficient to 
 16751  meet his or her burden of proof, an immigration officer will evaluate 
 16752  the individual case and make the determination as to whether additional 
 16753  evidence (such as a letter from a member of the school administration 
 16754  or faculty) is needed to adjudicate the case.
 16755      DHS also proposed to clarify that a student can qualify for a 
 16756  program extension and corresponding EOS based on a documented illness 
 16757  or medical condition. To provide an objective standard, DHS proposed to 
 16758  codify standards already included in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(B), which 
 16759  requires a student to provide medical documentation from a licensed 
 16760  medical doctor, licensed doctor of osteopathy, licensed psychologist, 
 16761  or licensed clinical psychologist to substantiate the illness or 
 16762  medical condition if seeking a reduced course load. See new 8 CFR 
 16763  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2). This is retained in the final rule. As this is 
 16764  already a long-standing requirement for DSOs and students in a similar 
 16765  context, DHS believes this will be appropriate and easy to implement in 
 16766  the program extension and corresponding EOS process. Further, requiring 
 16767  applicants to provide documentation of their medical illness or medical 
 16768  condition that caused their program delay is a reasonable request, 
 16769  because they are asking DHS to provide them additional time in the 
 16770  United States.
 16771      DHS also proposed a new factor in the EOS provisions--circumstances 
 16772  beyond the student's control, including a natural disaster, a national 
 16773  health crisis, or the closure of an institution. See new 8 CFR 
 16774  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(iii). This is retained in the final rule. As in 
 16775  the reinstatement context, DHS believes that there might be additional 
 16776  reasons beyond compelling academic or documented medical reasons that 
 16777  result in a student's inability to meet the program end date listed on 
 16778  the Form I-20.
 16779      Therefore, DHS proposed a third prong that encompasses scenarios 
 16780  that are not envisioned in the current provisions governing the 
 16781  extension of a program end date, such as those noted above. Some 
 16782  scenarios are currently in the reinstatement provisions, 8 CFR 
 16783  214.2(f)(16)(i)(F), such as natural disasters, pandemics, and the 
 16784  negligence of a DSO, and DHS believes that they merit favorable 
 16785  consideration in extension requests moving forward. Other scenarios may 
 16786  present circumstances that require a more intensive, fact-specific 
 16787  analysis and may fall into this proposed third prong. For example, the 
 16788  circumstances surrounding the closure of a school may be considered in 
 16789  determining whether the student qualifies for an EOS. By way of 
 16790  illustration, if a school closes as a result of a criminal conviction 
 16791  of its owners for engaging in student visa fraud by not requiring 
 16792  students to attend, but the student is unable to demonstrate that he or 
 16793  she was attending classes prior to closure as required to fulfill a 
 16794  full course of study, the closure of the institution might not qualify 
 16795  the student for a program extension. In contrast, if a school closes 
 16796  but a student is able to demonstrate that he or she was attending 
 16797  classes and was fulfilling all requirements to otherwise remain in 
 16798  status, the closure of the institute may qualify the student for a 
 16799  program extension.
 16800      The requirements to timely request an extension of the program end 
 16801  date would remain largely unchanged; however, DHS proposed a technical 
 16802  change to replace all references to the DSO ``granting'' an extension 
 16803  of the program with the term ``recommend'' an extension of the program 
 16804  in order for the student to file for EOS because USCIS, not the DSO,

**Assessing budget and resources**

Regarding Q11, there might be a fee around $675. I wonder how to best manage the search fees some numerals will incur. Let’s ensure I’m maximizing the resources while keeping everything organized!

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

   212  III. Background
   213  
   214  A. Legal Authority
   215  
   216      The authority to promulgate this rule rests on multiple, 
   217  independent, and mutually reinforcing statutory sources. The Secretary 
   218  of Homeland Security (Secretary) has broad authority under Section 102 
   219  of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 
   220  2135), 6 U.S.C. 112, and section 103(a)(1) and (3) of the Immigration 
   221  and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), to administer and 
   222  enforce the immigration and naturalization laws of the United States, 
   223  to include the issuance of regulations that he deems necessary.\1\ 
   224  Section 214(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), authorizes the Secretary 
   225  \2\ to prescribe the time and conditions of admission of any alien as a 
   226  nonimmigrant.
   227  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   228  
   229      \1\ Although provisions of the INA discussed in this NPRM refer 
   230  to the ``Attorney General,'' such provisions are now to be read as 
   231  referring to the Secretary of Homeland Security by operation of the 
   232  HSA. See 6 U.S.C. 202(3), 251.
   233      \2\ Although provisions of the INA discussed in this NPRM refer 
   234  to the ``Attorney General,'' such provisions are now to be read as 
   235  referring to the Secretary of Homeland Security by operation of the 
   236  HSA. See 6 U.S.C. 202(3), 251.
   237  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   238  
   239      In the INA, Congress established who may be admitted as F 
   240  nonimmigrants. Specifically, section 101(a)(15)(F) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 
   241  1101(a)(15)(F), established the F visa classification for bona fide 
   242  students who have a residence in a foreign country and wish to enter 
   243  the United States temporarily and solely for the purpose of pursuing a 
   244  full course of study at an academic or accredited language training 
   245  school. Participating schools must be certified by U.S. Immigration and 
   246  Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Student and Exchange Visitor Program 
   247  (SEVP).\3\ The authority to admit foreign students on a temporary basis 
   248  dates back to the Immigration Act of 1924, in which Congress first 
   249  established a student visa category similar to the modern F visa 
   250  classification, referring to ``[a]n immigrant who is a bona fide 
   251  student . . . who seeks to enter the United States solely for the 
   252  purpose of study at an accredited school . . . which shall have agreed 
   253  to report to the Secretary of Labor the termination of attendance of 
   254  each immigrant student. . . .'' \4\ In the decades that followed, 
   255  regulations codified a hands-on educational program for F-1 
   256  nonimmigrants related to their field of study, known as practical 
   257  training.
   258  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   259  
   260      \3\ See 8 CFR 214.3.
   261      \4\ Immig. Act of 1924, Public Law 68-139, 4(e), 43 Stat. 153, 
   262  155 (May 26, 1924); accord INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 
   263  1101(a)(15)(F)(i).
   264  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   265  
   266      The Secretary of DHS has the authority to regulate the time and 
   267  conditions of nonimmigrants' admission to the United States under INA 
   268  214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a).\5\ In the context of F-1 nonimmigrants, 
   269  setting the parameters of practical training has historically been 
   270  acknowledged as a valid exercise of DHS's statutory authority stemming 
   271  under the ``time-and-conditions'' provision in the INA.\6\ The period 
   272  of practical training prescribed by DHS through its regulations is 
   273  considered part of the ``time'' of an F-1 nonimmigrant's admission to 
   274  the United States, and the requirements for the training are part of 
   275  the ``conditions'' of such a status.\7\ Accordingly, DHS is authorized 
   276  to regulate under INA 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1), the ability for 
   277  F-1 nonimmigrant students to ``engage in limited periods of employment 
   278  for practical training . . . according to the terms set out in the 
   279  [OPT] [r]ule.'' \8\ The regulations governing F-1 nonimmigrants under 
   280  INA 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), are reasonably related to the purpose 
   281  of the visas issued under INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 
   282  1101(a)(15)(F)(i).\9\ Furthermore, the INA ``need not specifically 
   283  authorize each and every action taken by [DHS], so long as [such] 
   284  action is reasonably related to the duties imposed upon [the 
   285  Secretary].'' \10\ As part of the conditions of admission, DHS is now 
   286  setting a fee to ensure employers, students, and institutions are 
   287  engaging in appropriate activities consistent with admission as an F-1 
   288  nonimmigrant.\11\
   289  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   290  
   291      \5\ INA 103(a)(1), (3), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1).
   292      \6\ See Wash. All. of Tech. Workers v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland 
   293  Sec., 50 F.4th 164, 180-82 (D.C. Cir. 2022). See also Section 102 of 
   294  the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 
   295  2135), 6 U.S.C. 112, and section 103(a)(1) and (3) of the INA, 8 
   296  U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3).
   297      \7\ Wash. All. of Tech. Workers, 50 F.4th at 180-82.
   298      \8\ Id. at 169.
   299      \9\ Id. at 179.
   300      \10\ Narenji v. Civiletti, 617 F.2d 745, 747 (D.C. Cir. 1979).
   301      \11\ Id. at 168 (noting that while INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 
   302  U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F)(i), sets the terms of entry for F-1 
   303  nonimmigrant students, INA 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1), provides 
   304  DHS additional authority to regulate the ``time'' and ``conditions'' 
   305  of the students' stay where the regulation is reasonably related to 
   306  the terms of the F-1 visa).
   307  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   308  
   309      Within DHS, ICE administers SEVP and the Student and Exchange 
   310  Visitor Information System (SEVIS), which collects information related 
   311  to nonimmigrant students and exchange visitors and shares data with 
   312  other federal agencies with national security, immigration enforcement, 
   313  and immigration benefit adjudication responsibilities.\12\ This allows 
   314  government agencies to access essential information to preserve 
   315  national security and monitor immigration compliance.\13\ The Secretary 
   316  has authority to determine which aliens, including F-1 nonimmigrant 
   317  students, are ``authorized'' to obtain employment in the United 
   318  States.\14\
   319  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   320  
   321      \12\ See U.S. Immigration & Customs Enf't, Student and Exchange 
   322  Visitor Program, https://www.ice.gov/sevis (last updated Aug. 11, 
   323  2026).
   324      \13\ Id.
   325      \14\ See generally INA 274A(h)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3).
   326  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   327  
   328      As stated, DHS derives its authority to administer the programs in 
   329  which F nonimmigrant students engage, and the institutions that run 
   330  these programs, from several sources.\15\ Additionally, Section 641 of 
   331  the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 
   332  (IIRIRA) \16\ authorized the creation of a program for ongoing 
   333  collection of current information provided by schools and exchange 
   334  visitor programs regarding F and other nonimmigrants during the course 
   335  of their stays in the United States, using electronic reporting 
   336  technology where practicable. Consistent with this statutory authority, 
   337  DHS manages these programs pursuant to Homeland Security Presidential 
   338  Directive-2 (HSPD-2), Combating Terrorism Through Immigration Policies, 
   339  as amended,\17\ and Section 502 of the
   340  
   341  [[Page 64568]]
   342  
   343  Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act of 2002.\18\ HSPD-2 
   344  requires the Secretary to conduct periodic, ongoing reviews of schools 
   345  certified to accept F nonimmigrant students, and to include checks for 
   346  compliance with recordkeeping and reporting requirements.\19\ This 
   347  includes the ability for DHS to verify through records that an SEVP-
   348  certified institution has filed all appropriate paperwork and fees to 
   349  continue to participate in the SEVP program.\20\
   350  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   351  
   352      \15\ See Section 102 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (Pub. 
   353  L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135), 6 U.S.C. 112; INA 103(a)(1), (3), 8 
   354  U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3).
   355      \16\ Illegal Immig. Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 
   356  1996, Public Law 104-208, 110 Stat. 3009-546, 3009-704 (Sept. 30, 
   357  1996) (codified as amended at 8 U.S.C. 1372).
   358      \17\ Homeland Sec. Presidential Directive-2, Combating Terrorism 
   359  Through Immig. Policies (Oct. 29, 2001), available at https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2001/10/20011030-2.html [hereinafter Homeland Security Presidential Directive-2].
   360      \18\ Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act of 2002, 
   361  Public Law 107-173, 116 Stat. 543, 563 (May 14, 2002) (codified at 8 
   362  U.S.C. 1762).
   363      \19\ See Homeland Security Presidential Directive-2, supra note 
   364  17.
   365      \20\ Id.
   366  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   367  
   368      As part of DHS's authority to administer the programs F 
   369  nonimmigrant students engage in and regulate the institutions in which 
   370  they enroll, Section 502 of the Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry 
   371  Reform Act of 2002 directs the Secretary to review the compliance with 
   372  recordkeeping and reporting requirements under INA 101(a)(15), 8 U.S.C. 
   373  1101(a)(15)(F), and Section 641 of IIRIRA, 8 U.S.C. 1372, for all 
   374  schools approved for attendance by F-1 nonimmigrant students within two 
   375  years of enactment, and every two years thereafter. Moreover, as is the 
   376  case with all DHS programs, the programs discussed in this proposed 
   377  rule are carried out in keeping with DHS's primary mission, which 
   378  encompasses the responsibility to ``ensure that the overall economic 
   379  security of the United States is not diminished by the efforts, 
   380  activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland.'' \21\ DHS's 
   381  authority to regulate SEVP-certified institutions has historically 
   382  authorized regulations applying to educational institutions throughout 
   383  8 CFR 214, including requiring schools to file a petition for 
   384  certification and recertification, as the Secretary has deemed them 
   385  necessary to administer the program.\22\
   386  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   387  
   388      \21\ See 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F).
   389      \22\ E.g. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(A-C) (authorizing the DSO to

Document number:   2026-18631
Title:             Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period
Type:              Proposed Rule
Action:            Notice of proposed rulemaking.
Agencies:          Homeland Security Department
Citation:          91 FR 57807
Pages:             57807-57828 (22 pages)
Published:         2026-09-11
Comments close:    2026-11-10
Dates:             Written comments on the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) must be submitted on or before November 10, 2026. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will accept comments before midnight eastern time at the end of that day.
Docket:            CIS No. 2858-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364
RIN:               1615-AD22
CFR affected:      8 CFR 204, 8 CFR 214
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Adoption and foster care, Aliens, Cultural exchange programs, Employment, Foreign officials, Health professions, Immigration, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Students
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/11/2026-18631/eliminating-the-discretionary-60-day-grace-period
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-09-11/pdf/2026-18631.pdf

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes to remove regulations at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) to restore its previous and long- standing policy of not providing aliens in certain nonimmigrant classifications (and their dependents) with an up to 60-day grace period upon cessation of employment prior to the expiration of the alien's authorized period of stay. This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien's nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

    62                  Proclamation 11069 of September 18, 2026
    63  
    64                  
    65  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant 
    66                  Workers
    67  
    68                  By the President of the United States of America
    69  
    70                  A Proclamation
    71  
    72                  On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction 
    73                  on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 
    74                  Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses 
    75                  of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. The restrictions 
    76                  enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be 
    77                  highly effective but the underlying conditions 
    78                  necessitating the restrictions persist. It is therefore 
    79                  in the interests of the United States to extend the 
    80                  2025 Proclamation for an additional 12 months, until 
    81                  12:00 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2027.
    82  
    83                  As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B 
    84                  nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    85                  temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the 
    86                  United States, but it has been exploited to replace, 
    87                  not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. 
    88                  Certain employers, including information technology 
    89                  (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the 
    90                  system to suppress wages and displace American workers, 
    91                  and this has both harmed the labor market for American 
    92                  workers while also making it difficult to attract and 
    93                  retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT 
    94                  staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a 
    95                  large volume of entry-level temporary H-1B workers, 
    96                  generally at a much lower salary compared to full-time, 
    97                  traditional workers, and some of these firms later 
    98                  outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. 
    99                  This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign 
   100                  labor flooding the American labor market and making it 
   101                  difficult for American workers and recent graduates, 
   102                  especially in science, technology, engineering, and 
   103                  math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
   104  
   105                  To combat these abuses, the 2025 Proclamation set forth 
   106                  a restriction on entry of certain H-1B nonimmigrant 
   107                  workers, except for those petitions that were 
   108                  accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, 
   109                  subject to very limited exceptions. The 2025 
   110                  Proclamation went into effect on September 21, 2025, 
   111                  and, since then, the $100,000 payment has been made for 
   112                  over 700 petitions.
   113  
   114                  Additionally, the 2025 Proclamation required initiation 
   115                  of rulemakings by the Department of Homeland Security 
   116                  (DHS) and the Department of Labor (DOL) to address 
   117                  systemic H-1B program concerns. On December 29, 2025, 
   118                  DHS published a final rule, titled Weighted Selection 
   119                  Process for Registrants and Petitioners Seeking to File 
   120                  Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions, 90 Fed. Reg. 60864 (DHS 
   121                  final rule), to address the policy goals consistent 
   122                  with section 4(b) of the 2025 Proclamation. Through 
   123                  this rule, DHS created and implemented a weighted 
   124                  selection process that prioritizes the allocation of 
   125                  visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens to 
   126                  better protect the wages, working conditions, and job 
   127                  opportunities for American workers. This policy better 
   128                  serves the intent of the H-1B statutory scheme, 
   129                  incentivizes employers to recruit temporary workers for 
   130                  roles at the highest pay and skill levels, and was in 
   131                  effect for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 H-1B cap season. 
   132                  On March 27, 2026, DOL published a notice of proposed 
   133                  rulemaking, titled Improving Wage Protections for the 
   134                  Temporary and Permanent Employment of Certain Foreign 
   135                  Nationals in the United States, 91 Fed. Reg. 15454,
   136  
   137  [[Page 60498]]
   138  
   139                  to address the policy goals consistent with section 
   140                  4(a) of the 2025 Proclamation. The DOL's analysis of 
   141                  labor condition application data found that the average 
   142                  wage actually paid to H-1B workers, and the prevailing 
   143                  wage assigned to their positions, both remain well 
   144                  below the average wage earned by comparable American 
   145                  workers. The rule, once finalized, will better align 
   146                  prevailing wage levels with wages paid to similarly 
   147                  employed and located American workers and will 
   148                  strengthen overall program integrity. Finally, my 
   149                  Administration continues to explore other complementary 
   150                  efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B 
   151                  program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration 
   152                  program administration.
   153  
   154                  Since the effective date of the 2025 Proclamation and 
   155                  subsequent promulgation of the DHS final rule, there 
   156                  have been several measurable impacts on the H-1B 
   157                  program, including a significant reduction in H-1B 
   158                  registrations filed by large IT outsourcing firms, with 
   159                  the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms reducing 
   160                  their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, 
   161                  a 92 percent decrease. There has also been a large 
   162                  reduction in consular processing requests, which are 
   163                  used to bring workers into the United States, noting a 
   164                  nearly 97 percent decrease from the FY 2025 to FY 2027 
   165                  cap seasons. Finally, there has been a positive shift 
   166                  in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward 
   167                  higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with 
   168                  registrations for beneficiaries with at least a U.S. 
   169                  Master's degree rising from 45.1 percent of total 
   170                  registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1 percent for FY 2027. 
   171                  Job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest 
   172                  wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3 percent of 
   173                  H-1B registration selections while those corresponding 
   174                  with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8 
   175                  percent. It is reasonable to conclude that the required 
   176                  $100,000 payment and newly implemented weighted 
   177                  selection process have had the combined effect of 
   178                  deterring low-wage and low-skilled recruitment while 
   179                  increasing access for high-skilled and high-wage 
   180                  workers, as intended by the 2025 Proclamation.
   181  
   182                  Although the 2025 Proclamation and subsequent 
   183                  rulemaking have had the desired effects, the underlying 
   184                  conditions precipitating their issuance persist and, 
   185                  without an extension of the 2025 Proclamation, it is 
   186                  highly likely that progress will halt and program abuse 
   187                  will resume, undermining American workers and posing a 
   188                  threat to the labor market that would be detrimental to 
   189                  the interests of the United States. The 2025 
   190                  Proclamation highlighted a number of concerns, 
   191                  including high unemployment rates for recent graduates, 
   192                  wage suppression, fraud, and national security threats. 
   193                  Currently, these issues continue to undermine our 
   194                  economy, with unemployment rates for recent college 
   195                  graduates standing at 5.7 percent as of June 2026, a 
   196                  marginal decrease from September 2025, when the rate 
   197                  was 5.8 percent. Underemployment for recent college 
   198                  graduates also continues to cause concern, having risen 
   199                  from 41.8 percent in September 2025 to 42 percent as of 
   200                  June 2026. Additionally, while DOL is actively in the 
   201                  process of promulgating a rule to restore integrity to 
   202                  the prevailing wage system, it will take a significant 
   203                  amount of time to correct and balance the labor market. 
   204                  Finally, while fraud and abuse continue to be 
   205                  identified and investigated, these are ongoing and 
   206                  pervasive concerns that require a sustained, 
   207                  comprehensive response reflected in the entry 
   208                  restriction imposed by the 2025 Proclamation.
   209  
   210                  A review of the 2025 Proclamation's impacts and other 
   211                  recent policy changes has shown significant measurable 
   212                  changes in H-1B filing patterns that demonstrate the 
   213                  effectiveness of the 2025 Proclamation and a need for 
   214                  its extension. An extension of the 2025 Proclamation 
   215                  will continue to protect the economic and national 
   216                  security interests of the United States, improve labor 
   217                  market access for American workers and graduates, and 
   218                  ensure that employers recruit only the most highly-
   219                  skilled and essential alien workers when needed in line 
   220                  with the original intent of the program. As a result, 
   221                  the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, the 
   222                  Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland 
   223                  Security have jointly recommended an extension of the 
   224                  2025 Proclamation.
   225  
   226  [[Page 60499]]
   227  
   228                  As a result of these reviews and considerations, I have 
   229                  decided to continue to impose the limitations set forth 
   230                  in Proclamation 10973 on the entry into the United 
   231                  States by certain nonimmigrant workers. Accordingly, by 
   232                  the authority vested in me as President by the 
   233                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
   234                  America, it is hereby ordered:
   235  
   236                  Section 1. Restriction on Entry. (a) Pursuant to 
   237                  sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and 
   238                  Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1182(f) and 1185(a)), 
   239                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   240                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   241                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA 
   242                  (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b)), is restricted, except 
   243                  for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or 
   244                  supplemented by a payment of $100,000--subject to the 
   245                  exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this section. 
   246                  This restriction shall expire, absent extension, 12 
   247                  months after the effective date of this proclamation, 
   248                  which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   249                  September 21, 2026.
   250  
   251                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   252                  restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by a 
   253                  $100,000 payment for H-1B specialty occupation workers 
   254                  under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, who are 
   255                  currently outside the United States, for 12 months 
   256                  following the effective date of this proclamation as 
   257                  set forth in subsection (a) of this section.
   258                      (c) The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections 
   259                  (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any 
   260                  individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or 
   261                  all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of 
   262                  Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary's 
   263                  discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be 
   264                  employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the 
   265                  national interest and does not pose a threat to the 
   266                  security or welfare of the United States.
   267  
   268                  Sec. 2. Compliance. (a) Employers shall, prior to 
   269                  filing an H-1B petition on behalf of an alien outside 
   270                  the United States, obtain and retain documentation 
   271                  showing that the payment described in section 1 of this 
   272                  proclamation has been made.
   273  
   274                      (b) The Secretary of State shall verify receipt of 
   275                  payment of the amount described in section 1 of this 
   276                  proclamation during the H-1B visa petition process and 
   277                  shall approve only those visa applications for which 
   278                  the filing employer has made the payment described in 
   279                  section 1 of this proclamation.
   280                      (c) The Department of State and the Department of 
   281                  Homeland Security shall coordinate to take all 
   282                  necessary and appropriate action to implement this 
   283                  proclamation and to deny entry to the United States to 
   284                  any H-1B nonimmigrant for whom the prospective employer 
   285                  has not made the payment described in section 1 of this 
   286                  proclamation.
   287  
   288                  Sec. 3. Scope and Implementation of Restriction on 
   289                  Entry. (a) The restriction on entry pursuant to section 
   290                  1 of this proclamation shall apply only to aliens who 
   291                  enter or attempt to enter the United States after the 
   292                  effective date of this proclamation as set forth in 
   293                  section 1(a) of this proclamation. This restriction 
   294                  applies to aliens who must seek admission to the United 
   295                  States to effectuate the approval of a petition 
   296                  described in section 1 of this proclamation, including 
   297                  through consular notification, notification at a port 
   298                  of entry, pre-flight inspection, or pre-clearance.
   299  
   300                      (b) No later than 30 days following the completion 
   301                  of the H-1B lottery that immediately follows this 
   302                  proclamation, the Secretary of State, the Attorney 
   303                  General, the Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of 
   304                  Homeland Security shall jointly submit to the 
   305                  President, through the Assistant to the President and 
   306                  Homeland Security Advisor, a recommendation on whether 
   307                  an additional extension or renewal of the restriction 
   308                  on entry pursuant to section 1 of this proclamation is 
   309                  in the interests of the United States.
   310  
   311                  Sec. 4. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this 
   312                  proclamation shall be construed to impair or otherwise 
   313                  affect:
   314  
   315  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   316  the head thereof; or
   317  
   318  [[Page 60500]]
   319  
   320  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   321  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   322  
   323                      (b) This proclamation shall be implemented 
   324                  consistent with applicable law and subject to the 
   325                  availability of appropriations.
   326                      (c) This proclamation is not intended to, and does 
   327                  not, create any right or benefit, substantive or 
   328                  procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any 
   329                  party against the United States, its departments, 
   330                  agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or 
   331                  agents, or any other person.
   332  
   333                  IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this 
   334                  eighteenth day of September, in the year of our Lord 
   335                  two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the 
   336                  United States of America the two hundred and fifty-
   337                  first.

    26  Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency 
    27                  Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B 
    28                  Nonimmigrant Visa Program
    29  
    30                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    31                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    32                  America, it is hereby ordered:
    33  
    34                  Section 1. Purpose. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa program 
    35                  was created to identify uniquely skilled and highly 
    36                  specialized foreign temporary workers to strategically 
    37                  supplement the United States economy. Instead, the 
    38                  program has been widely abused by certain employers, 
    39                  third-party placement groups, and outsourcing firms to 
    40                  undercut and displace the supply of skilled United 
    41                  States labor. The large-scale, systematic abuse of the 
    42                  H-1B program to obtain non-qualifying foreign labor has 
    43                  undermined the additive purpose of the program and 
    44                  harmed the wages, working conditions, and job 
    45                  opportunities of skilled American workers.
    46  
    47                  The abuse of cheaper H-1B labor places downward 
    48                  pressure on domestic pay. H-1B visa holders earn far 
    49                  less than comparable United States-born workers, 
    50                  despite the statutory mandate that H-1B workers be paid 
    51                  equally to their domestic peers, with the estimated 
    52                  wage gap starting at $9,000 and climbing as high as 
    53                  $20,000 in H-1B reliant industries. One company even 
    54                  warned its shareholders that restrictions on cheap H-1B 
    55                  labor could force the company to use ``local'' workers, 
    56                  which ``may only be available at higher wages.''
    57  
    58                  Many employers have laid off large numbers of highly 
    59                  skilled American workers, only to promptly hire large 
    60                  numbers of H-1B workers who are often lower-skilled and 
    61                  lower-paid. For instance, technology sector employers 
    62                  have collectively requested H-1B visas for hundreds of 
    63                  thousands of workers, yet have also laid off somewhere 
    64                  between 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 
    65                  2022 through 2026. Employers have even forced laid off 
    66                  American workers to train their foreign replacements.
    67  
    68                  Many jobs held by H-1B workers eventually leave the 
    69                  United States entirely. Employers with outsourcing 
    70                  business models use teams of H-1B visa holders to 
    71                  replace United States workers at third-party client 
    72                  businesses and liaise with other individuals working 
    73                  off-site from their country of origin. As soon as 
    74                  practicable, much of their own work is transferred 
    75                  offshore. In Fiscal Year 2026, the top six users of the 
    76                  H-1B program operating with this outsourcing business 
    77                  model accounted for over 25,000 H-1B cap registrations. 
    78                  One foreign country's foreign minister even publicly 
    79                  admitted that H-1B ``has become the outsourcing visa.''
    80  
    81                  The systematic and organized abuse of the H-1B program 
    82                  is also a national security threat. Domestic law 
    83                  enforcement agencies have investigated H-1B-reliant 
    84                  outsourcing firms for engaging in visa fraud, 
    85                  conspiracy to launder money, and other illicit 
    86                  activities to encourage foreign workers to come to the 
    87                  United States. Abuses of the H-1B program also present 
    88                  a national security threat by discouraging Americans 
    89                  from pursuing careers in science and technology, 
    90                  risking vital United States leadership in these fields.
    91  
    92                  Numerous executive departments and agencies (agencies) 
    93                  have flagged employers' large-scale, systematic abuse 
    94                  of the H-1B program to obtain lower-paid, lower-skilled 
    95                  labor from abroad. These ongoing Government probes 
    96                  continue to identify widespread fraud and noncompliance 
    97                  among H-1B
    98

   101                  employers, such as: displacing American workers or 
   102                  otherwise giving preference to alien workers; 
   103                  misrepresenting the duties, requirements, or working 
   104                  conditions of job opportunities to avoid hiring or 
   105                  training American workers, falsely qualify jobs as 
   106                  specialty occupations, or lower applicable wage 
   107                  requirements; and misrepresenting aliens' 
   108                  qualifications to perform specialty occupations by 
   109                  submitting questionable foreign degrees from diploma

   115                  I have determined that continued efforts must be made

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending the regulations concerning the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for certain H-1B and L-1 Visas (9-11 Biometric Fee). The regulatory changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention and detection fee applies, which includes extension of status petitions that do not involve a change of employer. The 9-11 Biometric Fee continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of status. The changes also help DHS comply with its congressional mandate to implement a biometric entry-exit system.

Document number:   2025-16554
Title:             Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media
Type:              Proposed Rule
Action:            Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
Agencies:          Homeland Security Department
Citation:          90 FR 42070
Pages:             42070-42115 (46 pages)
Published:         2025-08-28
Comments close:    2025-09-29
Dates:             Comments must be received on or before September 29, 2025. Information collection comment period: Comments on the information collection described in the Paperwork Reduction Act section below must be received by October 27, 2025.
Docket:            DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001
RIN:               1653-AA95
Significant:       True
CFR affected:      8 CFR 214, 8 CFR 248, 8 CFR 274
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Aliens, Cultural exchange programs, Employment, Foreign officials, Health professions, Penalties, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Students
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/28/2025-16554/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-08-28/pdf/2025-16554.pdf

Abstract:
Unlike most nonimmigrant classifications, which are admitted for a fixed time period, aliens in the F (academic student), J (exchange visitor), and most I (representatives of foreign information media) classifications, with limited exceptions, are currently admitted into the United States for the period of time that they are complying with the terms and conditions of their nonimmigrant classification ("duration of status"). The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes to amend its regulations by changing the admission period in the F, J, and I classifications from duration of status to an admission for a fixed time period.

Use `toc`, `grep` or `text` with this document number to read the full text.

Abstract:

This final rule responds to comments received on the IFR and reaffirms and finalizes the provisions of the IFR. Abstract:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), which generally provides that USCIS gives deference to a prior approval involving the same facts when adjudicating a request to extend a petition for an alien's employment or stay. Receipt of means-tested public benefits before September 18, 2026 will be considered consistently with the 2022 Final Rule.
Docket:            CIS No. 2857-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0304
RIN:               1615-AD06
CFR affected:      8 CFR 103, 8 CFR 212
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Aliens, Authority delegations (Government agencies), Fees, Freedom of information, Immigration, Passports and visas, Privacy, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Surety bonds
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/20/2026-14539/public-charge-ground-of-inadmissibility
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/pdf/2026-14539.pdf

Abstract:
DHS is rescinding the 2022 public charge ground of inadmissibility regulations ("2022 Final Rule"). The 2022 Final Rule was not the best implementation of the statute. It was inconsistent with congressional intent, unduly restrictive, and hampered DHS's ability to make accurate, precise, and reliable determinations of whether certain aliens are likely at any time to become a public charge. Rescission restores broader discretion for DHS officers to evaluate all pertinent facts and aligns with long-standing policy that aliens in the United States should be self-reliant and government benefits should not incentivize immigration. This rule also revises the breach and cancellation of public charge bonds regulations.

 17603      Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), and 13563 
 17604  (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), direct agencies to assess 
 17605  the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if

 17612  regulations and provides that ``any new incremental costs associated
